decision.verdict: Pivot. The current build is competent craft aimed at the wrong verb: it asks the child to transcribe two numbers she has already been given into two dials, then type a product she can literally count off a tally strip that is printed on screen before she thinks. A visible clock punishes the deliberation the math requires, seven panels of chrome compete for a nine-year-old's attention, the right edge of the layout clips outside the 1365 frame, and the 'recount' help button states both factors outright. One genuinely strong idea is buried in there — judging a rival's false claim — and it deserves to become the spine of a new experience rather than a side mode inside a data-entry console. The pivot keeps the academic contract exactly and rebuilds the interaction so the child physically makes equal groups, watches them become an array, and sees the product become light in a sky that stays lit.
decision.strongestExistingQuality: The 'CALL THE BLUFF' beat. Handing the child an antagonist's stated equation and asking her to accept or reject it makes her the authority instead of the answer-typist, and it is the only place in the build where a representation is used as evidence rather than as decoration. That posture — prove the claim, catch the bad reasoning — is worth carrying forward.
decision.largestCreativeFailure: The experience reveals the answer before it asks the question and then rewards speed over thought. The tally strip displays g×e as countable tiles, the sentence hands over both factors, the dials only need matching, and the hint button says the factors aloud — so the child can complete every task without ever interpreting a multiplicative situation. On top of that, the math never causes anything: a claw drops, a counter increments, a stamp appears. Nothing in the world is built, changed, or kept by her reasoning, so there is no reason to want the next one.

creativeDirection.title: STARWRIGHT: Weave the Night
creativeDirection.openingPromise: The sky above the observatory is empty and black. A single gold spark drifts into the child's loom and the Sky Warden says: 'Stars are not found. They are woven — in equal nests, in even rows. Weave true and the constellation lights forever. Weave crooked and it falls dark.' She taps once, four sparks bloom into a nest, the nest snaps into a row, and the first tiny star ignites overhead. Whatever she lights stays lit for the rest of the night. Under thirty seconds, no instructions needed.
creativeDirection.coreLoop: One constellation at a time, in three visible beats. (1) GATHER — a Sky Order describes the weave ('The Heron needs 6 nests, 4 sparks in each'). She taps the spark loader to set how many sparks live in every nest, then taps to create nests; every nest fills to the same amount automatically, so equal groups are enforced by the material itself. (2) ALIGN — she pulls the loom lever and the loose nests slide into stacked rows, becoming an array: rows are the nests, row length is the amount in each. Each row lands with a rising pluck, so she hears the skip count. (3) SEAL — the equation strip below fills with her own rows × each, she keys the product, and taps SEAL. If the product is true, light races along the threads, the array collapses into a constellation and rises into the sky band at the top of the screen, permanently. Later beats invert the loop: sometimes she is handed a lit array and must read it, sometimes only a total and must invent the grouping, sometimes only a rival's claim and must build the proof.
creativeDirection.mathAsPower: The product is the light. The loom's glow meter fills to exactly the number of sparks she has actually woven, and a constellation only ignites when the sealed equation matches the sparks in the frame — so a wrong product is not marked wrong, it simply fails to light, and she can see the gap between what she claimed and what the frame holds. Nests visibly become rows, so equal-groups and array are the same object viewed twice. Nothing in the game can be counted one-by-one at higher stages: sparks inside sealed nests are opaque, clouds cover parts of read-the-sky arrays, and the audible row pluck rewards skip counting. Every star in the finished sky is a product she proved.
creativeDirection.stakes: A rival weaver, MIRRIK, is claiming sky. He is loud, fast, and sometimes sloppy: he broadcasts equations to stake a region ('8 nests of 3 — that's 21 stars, mine'). Any constellation she fails to weave, or any false claim she lets pass, gets shaded over with his violet haze — visible, named, and reclaimable. There is no countdown clock anywhere. The tension is territory on a sky she is watching fill up, not a timer beating her.
creativeDirection.consequenceAndRecovery: A wrong seal frays the weave: threads slacken, sparks drift loose, one nest cracks open to show its amount, and the frame stays there with her numbers intact so she can adjust rather than restart. Second attempt on the same constellation is always allowed, and the frayed attempt is never a permanent loss — it costs a shimmer of glow, not progress. If a constellation frays twice, Mirrik shades that patch, and it returns later as a RECLAIM order with slightly clearer framing, so a loss becomes an appointment rather than a wound. 'ASK THE LOOM' is available on every task and gives one graded step only — first press names which number is the count of nests and which is the amount inside, second press unpacks a single row and skip-counts it aloud in light, never the product. Hint use is logged in the ledger as 'guided', not as a penalty.
progression: STAGE 1 — FIRST LIGHT (3 orders, factors 2–5): both numbers stated plainly, nests carry visible spark counts, the loom shows a faint ghost lattice of the target array, and the equation strip pre-fills the two factors so only the product is hers. Teaches the vocabulary: nests = groups, sparks in each = amount, array = the same thing lined up.

STAGE 2 — READING THE SKY (3 orders, factors 3–7): the ghost lattice disappears and nests become opaque pods. Two of the three orders are reversed order-of-mention ('there are 5 sparks in every nest; the Lynx needs 7 nests') so she must decide which number is the groups. One order is a read-the-sky task: an already-lit array drifts overhead with a cloud across its middle — she states rows × each = product from the visible edges, without being able to count every star.

STAGE 3 — YOUR OWN WEAVE (3 orders, totals 12–48): only a total is given ('the Kite needs 24 stars, in equal nests — you choose'). Unequal nests physically jam the loom and the lever will not pull, so equality is discovered, not told. Any valid factor pair lights the constellation; a second different pair for the same total earns a bonus twin star and the Warden notes 'two true weaves, same sky.'

STAGE 4 — MIRRIK'S CLAIMS (3 orders, factors 3–9): he states a situation and a product. She must weave the proof array first, then rule TRUE or FALSE and key the true product. Two of his three claims are wrong in tempting ways (off by one group, off by the amount in one nest, or a swapped-then-miscounted product); one is correct, so 'always call him a liar' fails. Busting a false claim tears his haze off a shaded region.

STAGE 5 — TOWERS (2 orders, nested, totals ≤ 60): three-part situations ('4 towers, each tower holds 3 nests, each nest 5 sparks'). She weaves one tower's array, the loom copies it as many times as needed, and the equation strip accepts a chain — she must decide what to multiply first and can solve it either way, with the loom showing both groupings agree.

STAGE 6 — THE GREAT CONSTELLATION (finale, 1 multi-panel order): three linked weaves with every scaffold off, no visible spark counts, one hint total available, and the third panel's grouping chosen by her. Completing it fires the whole sky.
creativeDirection.worldReaction: Every beat answers back. Adding a nest makes a soft chime one step higher than the last; aligning plays a rising run of notes exactly as long as the amount in each nest; a true seal sends light up the threads, lifts the constellation into the sky band, and the Warden names it in a short line of speech. The sky band is a real ledger — after four constellations the horizon glows, after eight the observatory dome opens, after twelve the water below reflects the whole map. Mirrik reacts too: he crows when a weave frays, goes quiet and smaller when busted, and his haze visibly peels back off reclaimed sky. Stars she lit early keep twinkling in the background of every later task, so the screen becomes a record of her own work.
creativeDirection.payoff: At the end the loom goes dark and the camera pulls up into the full sky. Every constellation she wove lights in sequence, and as each ignites its equation writes itself in gold beneath it — '6 × 4 = 24 · The Heron' — with the audible skip count replaying underneath, so the finale is a review of her own reasoning rather than a score screen. Mirrik's last haze burns off. Then the biggest unnamed constellation blinks and the Warden asks her to name it; she types a name and it is stitched permanently into the sky map with the words 'Woven by [name], Starwright.' A single line of honest summary follows: how many constellations she lit, how many claims she overturned, and the hardest weave she solved with no hint.
creativeDirection.replay: 'NEXT NIGHT' reseeds a different sky region: new constellation silhouettes, new contexts, and a fresh problem pool that guarantees no factor pair and no situation wording repeats within a night or from the previous night — repeats are treated as a bug, not variety. Mirrik returns for a REMATCH night with the difficulty floor raised: scaffolds off from the first order, factors to 10, judging and nested weaves doubled, and two new order types — 'prove it two ways' (commutativity: the same total woven as rows-of-x and rows-of-y) and 'the sabotaged weave' (an array arrives with one row short and she must say what it truly shows versus what it claims). Named sky maps from earlier nights stay visible as faint background constellations, so the sky is cumulative across sessions.
creativeDirection.visualAndSoundDirection: Warm-dark, hand-made, no console chrome. Background: deep indigo to violet vertical gradient with a black silhouette treeline and a brass observatory rail along the bottom. The loom is drawn as a warm wooden frame with brass pins and thin luminous threads; nests are soft gold orbs with a woven texture; sparks are small radiant dots with a bloom halo — no emoji anywhere. Type is a rounded warm serif for the Warden's voice and a clean sans for numbers only. Palette limited to indigo, brass gold, star white, and Mirrik's cold violet, so 'his sky' versus 'her sky' reads instantly. Touch targets are large and few: at most one lever, one loader, one keypad, and two decision buttons on screen at a time. Sound is acoustic and quiet: marimba plucks for nests, a harp run for row alignment, a warm three-note chord swell for ignition, a low wooden thud and slackening thread for a fray (never a buzzer), Mirrik as a short pitched-down brass sting, and a slow ambient pad that gains one instrument layer per completed stage so the night audibly fills up alongside the sky.

decision.opusBuilderBrief:
Build STARWRIGHT: Weave the Night as a single self-contained HTML file, 1365×768 fixed, no external assets, no libraries, all art in CSS/SVG/canvas, all sound via WebAudio oscillators (marimba-ish triangle plucks, no harsh square buzzers). Every interaction must work with a single tap or click; drag is optional garnish only, never required. Nothing may extend past x=1365 or y=768 — verify the right column and bottom bar fit before styling.

LAYOUT (fixed regions, never scrolling):
- SKY BAND y 0–232, full width: canvas or absolutely positioned SVG. Holds permanently lit constellations (each a small cluster of dots plus a thin connecting line and a gold equation caption at 13px), Mirrik's violet haze patches, and the current constellation's faint dotted silhouette as the target slot. Background gradient indigo→violet, slow twinkle animation, treeline silhouette at its base.
- SKY ORDER CARD x 24–392, y 252–472: the situation text at 24px on warm parchment, key phrases tinted (groups in cool gold, amount-in-each in warm amber). Below it, y 486–744, THE LEDGER: a compact list of proved equations this night, newest first, 15px, marked 'guided' if a hint was used.
- THE LOOM x 412–1000, y 252–620: a wooden/brass frame. Top third is the GATHER TRAY where created nests appear in a wrapping row; bottom two thirds is the LATTICE where nests become rows of sparks after alignment. Rows must always render as evenly spaced horizontal rows with equal spark counts; cap the display at 10 rows × 10 sparks and size sparks so 10×10 fits comfortably.
- CONTROL STACK x 1016–1341, y 252–744: SPARK LOADER (large −/+ with a big numeral, label 'SPARKS IN EACH NEST'), ADD NEST button, PULL LOOM lever, ASK THE LOOM button, and a 3×4 numeric keypad for the product. Judge tasks swap the lever for TRUE / FALSE buttons.
- EQUATION STRIP x 412–1000, y 636–744: reads [rows] × [each] = [product input], 40px, auto-filled from the frame's actual state, with the SEAL button at its right. Rows and each are never typed by the child — they are read off the weave she built, which is the point.

TASK TYPES (implement all six; keep every task solvable in 20–60 seconds):
1. BUILD_FROM_SITUATION — text gives groups and amount; she sets the loader, adds nests, pulls the loom, keys the product, seals.
2. READ_ARRAY — an array is pre-lit in the sky band with a cloud rectangle covering interior rows; she reads rows and columns from the exposed edges and keys the product. No counting path exists through the cloud.
3. CHOOSE_GROUPING — only a total is given; she picks any factor pair. If loader × nests ≠ total the lever refuses to pull and the loom shakes with a soft wooden creak plus the message 'the nests are not even'. Award a bonus twin star for a second, different valid pair on the same total.
4. JUDGE_CLAIM — Mirrik states a situation and a product; she must build the proof array first (TRUE/FALSE stay disabled until the frame matches the stated situation), then rule and key the true product. Wrong claims must be off by one group, off by the amount in one nest, or a plausible near-miss — never off by a wild amount. Exactly one claim per stage set is TRUE.
5. NESTED — three-part situation (towers × nests × sparks, total ≤ 60). She weaves one tower's array, presses COPY TOWER, the loom duplicates it, and the equation strip accepts (a×b)×c in either order; show both partial products agreeing.
6. RECLAIM — a regenerated version of a previously frayed or lost task with slightly plainer wording, appearing 2–3 tasks later. Success visibly peels Mirrik's haze off that sky patch.

SEQUENCE: 15 tasks total, ordered exactly as the six stages in progression, ending with the three-panel finale. Store every used factor pair, total, context noun set, and wording template in a session set and never reuse any of them; also persist the previous night's set in memory for the replay pass. Verify all generated arithmetic in code (product must equal groups × each; nested totals must equal the chain) before rendering.

SCAFFOLD FADE (this is the independence requirement, implement it literally): Stage 1 shows spark counts printed on nests, a ghost lattice of the target array, and pre-filled factors in the equation strip. Stage 2 removes the ghost lattice and the printed counts. Stage 3 removes pre-filled factors. Stage 4 onward removes the tally of loose sparks entirely. Nowhere, at any stage, may the product appear on screen before the child seals it — no tally strip, no count readout that equals the answer.

FEEDBACK RULES: On a true seal — light travels the threads over ~700ms, the array lifts and reforms as a constellation in the sky band with its equation caption, a three-note warm chord, and one line of Warden speech that restates the structure ('six nests of four — twenty-four lights, and they stay'). On a fray — threads slacken, sparks scatter but the frame keeps her numbers, one nest cracks open showing its amount, a low wooden thud, and a message that describes the mismatch without giving the answer ('your frame holds six rows of four; you sealed 22 — walk the rows again'). Two frays on one task shade the patch and schedule a RECLAIM. ASK THE LOOM gives step one (names which number is the groups and which is the amount in each), then step two (unpacks a single row and skip-counts it in light and sound), and never the product.

AUDIO: adding a nest plays a pluck rising one step per nest; pulling the loom plays an ascending run with exactly as many notes as the amount in each nest (the audible skip count); ignition is a warm major chord; fray is a low thud plus a detuned slide; Mirrik is a short pitched-down sting. Keep all gains ≤0.2 and wrap WebAudio in try/catch. Add a mute toggle in the top right of the sky band.

FINALE: fade the loom, pan the sky, ignite each constellation in the order it was won with its equation writing itself beneath and its skip-count replaying, burn off remaining haze, then a naming prompt (text input, 16 chars, sanitized) that stitches 'Woven by [name], Starwright' into the map. Show an honest three-line summary: constellations lit, claims overturned, hardest weave solved unaided. Offer NEXT NIGHT (new seed, no repeats) and MIRROR MATCH (harder night: scaffolds off from task one, factors to 10, doubled judge and nested tasks, plus two new types — prove-it-two-ways commutativity and a sabotaged array that is one row short of its claim).

CONSTRAINTS TO RESPECT: no countdown timers anywhere; no punishment for hint use; touch targets ≥ 56px tall for all primary controls; text at 20px or larger for anything the child must read to reason; at most one decision surface and one build surface active at a time; and total playtime 9–13 minutes from opening to payoff.
